tldr: When training autonomous-driving VLA models with reinforcement learning, groups where all sampled rollouts fail pose a major challenge. The authors propose "FIRE-VLA," a method that applies self-distillation from a same-scale teacher model conditioned on the ground-truth future trajectory specifically for such failure groups. Compared to standard GRPO, it preserves normal trajectory planning performance while significantly reducing catastrophic failures and persistent failures.
hero_caption: Overview of FIRE-VLA. In predicting future trajectories from front-camera images and history, standard GRPO can output abnormally scaled trajectories in difficult scenes, whereas FIRE-VLA prevents such catastrophic collapse. Across the held-out nuScenes evaluation set, it reduces evaluation-persistent failure prevalence from 13.03% to 11.20% and lowers the mean error under four rollouts.
overview:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used for the post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) models in autonomous driving. In particular, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—which samples multiple rollouts per prompt and learns from reward differences within the group—is an attractive method that eliminates the need for an independent value model. However, it has a critical weakness: when all sampled trajectories within a group are poor failures, GRPO can only rank failures against each other ("better failures" vs. "worse failures") without providing any signal on how to escape the failed region.

To solve this, the authors introduce "FIRE-VLA," a failure-informed self-evolution framework where the model learns from unresolved failures without relying on a larger external teacher model. The idea is simple and clever: it automatically detects "unresolved failure groups" with low rewards and low diversity, and applies self-distillation only to these groups using a frozen copy of the model itself from the start of the round as a "privileged teacher." This teacher model has the exact same parameter scale as the student, but it receives the hidden future ground-truth trajectory as privileged information. Furthermore, distillation is applied strictly to the output trajectory tokens conditioned on the student's own generated reasoning prefix, preventing distribution shifts. When a round finishes, the updated student becomes the teacher for the next round, repeating this self-evolution cycle.

Rigorous evaluations on 6,019 samples from 150 held-out nuScenes scenes show that FIRE-VLA retains comparable single-sample planning performance while reducing the mean L2 error under 4 stochastic rollouts by 18.8%, from 1.848 m to 1.500 m. Analyses reveal that this improvement stems not from a uniform uplift across ordinary cases, but from strongly suppressing rare, catastrophic rollout failures.
contributions: Formulated the problem of "unresolved failure groups," where all trajectories in a group have low rewards and low diversity, making it difficult to escape using relative reward signals alone.

Developed "privileged self-distillation" (PSD), which does not rely on a larger external model but provides the same model with the future ground-truth trajectory, applying distillation selectively to student-generated trajectory tokens.
Proposed a round-based self-evolution framework (FIRE-VLA) that promotes the teacher and updates the routed failure distribution as the policy evolves.

Demonstrated on held-out nuScenes scenes that the method significantly reduces evaluation-persistent failure prevalence (from 13.03% to 11.20%) and suppresses extreme catastrophic tails without degrading normal trajectory planning performance.

sections.heading: How do we escape groups where every rollout fails?
sections.summary: In RL training for autonomous-driving VLAs, GRPO learns from relative rewards, but groups where all sampled rollouts fail provide no guidance on how to improve. FIRE-VLA resolves this by applying self-distillation from a same-scale privileged teacher that observes future trajectories, targeting only these unresolved failure groups.
sections.details:
VLA models that map vision and language directly to actions are rapidly advancing in autonomous driving. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning on policy-generated rollouts can further boost performance. Recently, GRPO has attracted significant attention because it avoids training an independent value network (unlike PPO) and instead learns from relative reward differences across multiple rollouts sampled from the same input.

However, there is a catch. When sampled rollouts contain a mix of successes and failures, GRPO works well. But in difficult scenarios, all generated rollouts may end up as severe failures. In this case, relative rewards only rank failures within the group without providing an explicit corrective signal to escape the failed region. While gradients do not vanish to zero, the necessary guidance to escape is fundamentally missing.

FIRE-VLA addresses this core issue. It detects failure groups characterized by low rewards and low diversity online and injects privileged self-distillation (PSD) specifically into those groups. Rather than using a giant external model, it freezes a copy of itself from the start of the round as the teacher and provides only that teacher with the "hidden future ground-truth trajectory." Evaluated on nuScenes under strictly matched student rollouts and policy updates against baseline GRPO, FIRE-VLA substantially reduces catastrophic errors and persistent failures.

sections.heading: At the intersection of VLAs, relative-reward RL, and failure-driven learning
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work on autonomous-driving VLAs, post-training with GRPO, and self-distillation. FIRE-VLA unifies these threads by combining failure-based routing with privileged self-distillation using a same-scale model.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main lines:

- Autonomous-driving VLA models: Multimodal integration has progressed rapidly, including language-guided driving (LMDrive), scene-graph reasoning (DriveLM), and trajectory generation (CoVLA, SimLingo). This paper uses open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct as a shared backbone, focusing on the post-training algorithm rather than novel model architectures.

- Relative-reward reinforcement learning: GRPO normalizes rewards across multiple outputs for the same prompt, eliminating the need for a separate value network. It has begun to be applied to autonomous-driving VLAs (e.g., AutoDrive-R2), but the lack of corrective signals when an entire group fails remained an unaddressed challenge.

- Failure-aware learning and privileged self-teaching: Methods like ELF-VLA identify past failures to provide corrective feedback, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both student and privileged teacher. FIRE-VLA combines automatic failure routing, privileged distillation on top of student-generated prefixes, and round-based teacher promotion to achieve self-evolution without requiring external models.

sections.heading: How FIRE-VLA works: Selective self-distillation via a privileged teacher
sections.summary: FIRE-VLA detects groups with low rewards and low diversity, and distills trajectory tokens from a frozen teacher of the same scale provided with the ground-truth future trajectory. As training rounds proceed, the updated student becomes the next teacher, adapting the supervision to newly unresolved failure regions.
sections.details:
Training in FIRE-VLA consists of repeating self-evolution rounds across four stages:

3.1 Trajectory Learning with Relative Rewards
The input is a front-camera image $I_i$ and ego history $h_i$. The model outputs a reasoning process followed by 6-step waypoints in local coordinates (at 0.5 s intervals, spanning 3.0 s) enclosed in `<answer>` tags. The reward $r$ is computed via an inverse function of the L2 error relative to the ground-truth trajectory (invalid formatting receives zero reward). GRPO samples rollouts with group size $G$ ($G=4$ in this work) and normalizes advantages using the group mean and standard deviation.

3.2 Failure-Informed Routing
For each group, the mean reward $\bar{r}_i$, standard deviation $\sigma_i$, and valid format rate $v_i$ are computed. Within a minibatch, groups with $v_i \ge 0.5$ whose mean reward falls into the bottom 30% and standard deviation falls into the bottom 30% are classified as "unresolved failure groups." A low mean indicates failure, while low variance indicates that relative reward signals are unhelpful. Distillation signals are routed exclusively to these groups.

3.3 Privileged Future Trajectory Injection
The teacher model $\pi_{\bar{\theta}_k}$ starts with identical weights to the student $\pi_{\theta_k}$ and is frozen during the round. While the student only receives images and history, the teacher prompt includes the "hidden future ground-truth trajectory" as privileged information. Crucially, the teacher is fed the exact token prefix generated by the student and predicts the continuation distribution, preventing off-policy distributional divergence.

3.4 On-Policy Answer-Token Distillation
Distillation is restricted strictly to the trajectory tokens inside the `<answer>` tags generated by the student. Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence is computed over a compact distribution consisting of the teacher's top-16 tokens plus residual probability. The overall loss adds this trajectory token distillation loss (weighted by $\lambda=0.1$) on routed groups to the standard GRPO loss applied to all groups.

3.5 Round-Based Self-Evolution
In this study, each round comprises 75 updates, running for a total of two rounds ($K=2$). The updated student from Round 1 becomes the starting weights for Round 2, and the teacher is replaced by this model. As the policy evolves, the distribution of "where unresolved failures occur" dynamically shifts accordingly.

sections.heading: Validation on nuScenes: Dramatically curbing catastrophic tail risks
sections.summary: Using Qwen2.5-VL-3B on 150 held-out nuScenes scenes (6,019 samples), FIRE-VLA was compared against standard GRPO. While preserving single-sample planning performance, it reduced the mean L2 error under 4 stochastic rollouts from 1.848 m to 1.500 m and significantly lowered the persistent failure rate from 13.03% to 11.20%.
sections.details:
4.1 Experimental Setup
The base model was an SFT checkpoint of Qwen2.5-VL-3B, trained using FSDP (full-parameter BF16) across 4 RTX 3090 GPUs. GRPO and FIRE-VLA were strictly matched on unique prompts (1,200), total rollouts (4,800), and policy updates (150). Evaluation was conducted on 6,019 samples drawn from 150 nuScenes scenes completely held out from pre-training and SFT. Metrics evaluated L2 errors under low-temperature (temp 0.2) single rollouts and stochastic (temp 0.8) 4-rollout ($G=4$) sampling.

4.2 Primary Trajectory Planning Results
In single rollouts (Table 1), FIRE-VLA achieved a mean L2 error of 0.602 m compared to 0.642 m for GRPO; however, the scene-clustered 95% confidence interval crosses zero, indicating comparable normal planning performance. In contrast, under 4 stochastic rollouts (Table 2), a clear difference emerged: FIRE-VLA's mean L2 error was 1.500 m, an 18.8% reduction compared to GRPO's 1.848 m (difference $-0.3476$ m, 95% CI $[-0.7711, -0.0319]$).

4.3 Impact of Learning from Unresolved Failures
Applying a persistent failure detector defined and frozen on SFT data, 13.03% of all samples (784 cases) were flagged as persistent failures under GRPO, whereas FIRE-VLA reduced this to 11.20% (674 cases) (difference $-1.83$ percentage points, 95% CI $[-2.55, -1.11]$). Furthermore, the proportion of samples containing catastrophic rollouts with errors $\ge 10$ m dropped substantially from 1.35% to 0.83%.

4.4 Qualitative Analysis
As shown in Figure F3, in challenging cases such as nighttime curves where GRPO errors worsen (a), FIRE-VLA restores trajectory quality to SFT levels. In persistent failure cases (b) or high-variance cases (c), FIRE-VLA reliably maintains stable driving trajectories.

captions.F3: Qualitative comparison across four representative scenes: (a) a case where GRPO error worsened, (b) a persistent failure in GRPO resolved by FIRE-VLA, (c) a case where variance was restrained, and (d) a counterexample where GRPO performed better. Green indicates ground truth, blue is GRPO, and orange is FIRE-VLA.

sections.heading: Why it works, and what the current limitations are
sections.summary: The strength of FIRE-VLA lies in efficiently injecting ground-truth trajectory guidance tailored to the model's own failures without relying on a larger external teacher. At the same time, the authors candidly discuss limitations such as added compute and open-loop evaluation.
sections.details:
The discussion elaborates on why this method works and where its boundaries lie:

- Role of failure routing: In healthy groups containing both good and bad samples, standard GRPO is optimal. Intervening with privileged distillation only when an entire group fails rescues the policy from dead ends without suppressing RL exploration.

- Advantages of a same-scale teacher: Conditioning on the ground-truth future trajectory in context creates a powerful teacher without expanding parameter count. Moreover, conditioning on the student's reasoning prefix preserves contextual alignment. At test time, the privileged teacher branch is completely discarded, incurring zero deployment overhead.

- Limitations:
1. Fairness of comparison: While unique prompts and update counts are strictly matched, FIRE-VLA requires additional teacher forward passes and resets the optimizer state between rounds, meaning it is not a strictly equal-compute comparison.
2. Single seed: Results are based on a single training seed, and run-to-run variance is not reflected in the confidence intervals.
3. Open-loop evaluation: Evaluation is restricted to static trajectory prediction on front-camera images (open loop); safety, ride comfort, and cumulative drift in closed-loop environments where ego actions affect the world remain unmeasured.

sections.heading: Takeaway: Self-evolution that tames tail risks
sections.summary: FIRE-VLA effectively curbs rare, catastrophic trajectory failures by applying privileged self-distillation to all-failure groups where GRPO struggles. Self-evolution within the same model scale offers a practical pathway toward building reliable autonomous-driving models.
sections.details: FIRE-VLA presents an elegant solution to the fundamental problem of unresolved failures that relative reward ranking cannot fix: privileged self-distillation from a same-scale model combined with round-based evolution. Over two rounds of validation, it demonstrated substantial reductions in catastrophic errors and persistent failures without harming ordinary driving accuracy. Future work will explore running additional self-evolution rounds and testing under closed-loop simulation environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Error distribution details and the "reward trap"
sections.summary: Detailed statistical analyses demonstrate that the reduction in mean L2 error stems not from lifting ordinary cases, but from suppressing extreme failure tails. The authors also highlight how scalar rewards saturate with respect to large geometric errors.
sections.details:
The appendix provides critical data for understanding the experimental results:

- Error tail analysis (Appendices A, E): Analyzing all 24,076 candidate rollouts, GRPO is actually slightly better at the median (0.550 m vs. 0.598 m) and the 90th percentile (1.498 m vs. 1.594 m). However, at the 99th percentile (2.926 m vs. 2.881 m) and especially in CVaR99—the conditional expectation of the worst 1%—FIRE-VLA is overwhelmingly superior (118.58 m vs. 79.21 m). Comparisons using Winsorized means with error cutoffs further confirm that FIRE-VLA's mean L2 error reduction is driven by suppressing rare wild deviations exceeding 10 m.

- Discrepancy between scalar rewards and L2 error (Appendix C): In terms of mean scalar reward alone, GRPO (0.6370) outperforms FIRE-VLA (0.6156). This occurs because the reward function (an inverse transformation) rapidly saturates toward zero in regions with large geometric errors. Whether an error is 10 m or 100 m, the reward is virtually zero and indistinguishable. Consequently, GRPO chased slightly higher rewards on ordinary cases while harboring a catastrophic long tail of extreme failures.

takeaways: Relative-reward RL methods like GRPO cannot provide an escape signal when all sampled rollouts in a group fail.
Without an external giant model, a frozen copy of the same model conditioned on the ground-truth future trajectory provides a strong privileged distillation signal.

The dramatic reduction in mean L2 error comes not from a uniform boost across normal trajectories, but from curbing rare catastrophic runaway rollouts (tail risks), which is vital for autonomous-driving safety.
Saturating scalar rewards (e.g., inverse-error mappings) risk masking extreme geometric errors, making tail distribution metrics (such as CVaR) essential during evaluation.
limitations: Compute resources (FLOPs and wall-clock training time) are not completely identical to GRPO due to additional teacher forward passes and optimizer resets between rounds.
Evaluation is confined to open-loop trajectory prediction on pre-recorded logs; cascading closed-loop interactions in simulators have not been validated.
Experiments were conducted with a single random seed, meaning training run-to-run variability was not assessed.
